records.name: Sīmanis

The Siliņš catalogue records a historical detail: Mārciena, 1562; calendar 1767 (dictionary page 291). This dates an attributed record of use or calendar inclusion. It does not mean that the name was created then; a date attached to a shared entry retains that shared scope.

records.name: Gaudentas
records.facts_used: The dictionary explains Gaudentas as a short form of Gaudencijus and pairs that full name with Gaudentius. This establishes the Lithuanian full-name and short-name chain without needing to infer a meaning from similar-looking words. The exact form is documented in the Senn–Salys Lithuanian–German dictionary of 1968, reprinted in Salys’s collected writings in 1983. This is a dated linguistic record of the name and its relationships; it does not identify the first child registered with this spelling.

records.name: Vytautė
records.facts_used: Vytautė is the feminine form in the Vytautas family. The traditional element analysis links Vyt- with vyti, “to chase”, and Taut- with tauta, “people, nation”; these elements are not a literal description of a woman bearing the name. Sinkevičiūtė’s linguistic review corrects Vitautė to Vytautė; Pakerys also discusses the exact feminine form in 2011. These scholarly records preserve the initial Vy-. They do not transfer the medieval male ruler’s life dates to the feminine name.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Sinkevičiūtė PDF 3 / printed 275; Pakerys PDF 4 / printed 93; Salys PDF 296–297 / printed 281–282. Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Lea
records.facts_used: Gulbrand Alhaug explains Lea as a Hebrew feminine name associated with the word for a wild cow. He distinguishes its early association with Latin lea, “lioness”. The Latin association is not the sole established origin of the Hebrew name. Rajandi’s 1966 Estonian dictionary records Lea as popular in 1958–1960 and groups it with Lia and Liia. His Latin explanation reflects the lioness association. Reading it alongside the Hebrew account preserves the difference between origin and later interpretation.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.
records.uncertainties: Checked location: Rajandi PDF 102 / printed 104; Alhaug signed opening etymology, updated 28 May 2024. Original PDF pages were visually read where used; catalogue transcriptions remain attributed.

records.name: Leana
records.facts_used: Rajandi describes Leana as an analogical development in the Lea/Lia group. He separately compares Liana and Liane, which can come from Juliane. His comparison does not make every Leana a Juliane short form. The form and its relationships are documented in Edgar Rajandi’s Raamat nimedest, published in Tallinn in 1966. The book records the naming traditions known at that time. Its publication date documents a linguistic treatment, rather than the name’s invention or its first birth registration.
records.reason: Exact-form evidence supports a reviewed history in five languages.

records.name: Liia
records.facts_used: Rajandi groups Liia with Lea and Lia, noting Russian Лия as an influence on the spelling. This is a documented naming relationship. The later Latin “lioness” association of Lea should not replace the Hebrew background of the wider family. Mägiste’s 1929 Estonian name list already prints the exact spelling Liia and cites Wiedemann. Rajandi discusses it again in 1966. These are dated dictionary records of Liia itself, rather than dates transferred from a different spelling.
